technique.how: Inspect the supine abdomen from the side and foot of the bed for a protuberant contour, flank bulging and visible loops or peristalsis. Percuss all quadrants: tympany suggests gas-filled bowel (obstruction/ileus), suprapubic dullness a full bladder, flank dullness fluid. Ask the patient whether the belly feels bigger than usual.
technique.prerequisites: Supine patient with abdomen fully exposed; compare with baseline habitus if known.

interpretation.positive_finding: New tympanitic distension with pain and vomiting points to small bowel obstruction (RR ~13 vs no distension in the OMGE series); tense distension with oliguria raises abdominal compartment syndrome; suprapubic dullness suggests retention.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of distension makes complete SBO less likely but does not exclude proximal or early obstruction, ischemia or perforation.
interpretation.pitfalls: Obesity, ascites, pregnancy and chronic constipation mimic or mask distension; a tense abdomen from retention is easily mistaken for obstruction. Percussion note and contour are poorly reproducible between examiners.
interpretation.changes_what: Distension + pain/vomiting: NG decompression, fluids, CT abdomen. Tense distension with AKI: measure bladder pressure. Suprapubic dullness: bladder scan and catheterize.

sources.citation: Eskelinen M, Ikonen J, Lipponen P. Contributions of history-taking, physical examination, and computer assistance to diagnosis of acute small-bowel obstruction. A prospective study of 1333 patients with acute abdominal pain. Scand J Gastroenterol. 1994;29(8):715-721.
Taylor MR, Lalani N. Adult small bowel obstruction. Acad Emerg Med. 2013;20(6):528-544.

Bohner H, Yang Q, Franke C, Verreet PR, Ohmann C. Simple data from history and physical examination help to exclude bowel obstruction and to avoid radiographic studies in patients with acute abdominal pain. Eur J Surg. 1998;164(10):777-784.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not interpret distension in isolation in patients with ascites, pregnancy, or known chronic megacolon; do not use absence of distension to defer imaging when pain is severe or peritoneal signs exist.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Distension with peritonism, hemodynamic instability, or rising lactate suggests strangulation or perforation: immediate surgical review. Tense abdomen with oliguria: check intra-abdominal pressure.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Reported as a best predictor in three SBO series, but grading of distension is subjective and reproducibility data are lacking.

extraction_notes: Taylor & Lalani 2013 (Acad Emerg Med) pooled sensitivity/specificity/LR for distension are in tables not accessible through PubMed/PMC (journal not open access), so no pooled numbers are entered; abstract confirms distension was among the best exam predictors. Bohner 1998 abstract names distended abdomen among the six most sensitive variables without numbers. The only visible number is Eskelinen 1994 relative risk 13.1 (not an LR; sens/spec fields left null). A verifier with journal access should replace with the pooled LR+/LR- from Taylor & Lalani Table.
